entities.name: Childeric III
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Childeric III, born around 717 CE, reigned as the final king of the Frankish Merovingian dynasty from 743 until his deposition in 751. His brief and largely nominal rule marked the terminal decline of a lineage that had governed the Franks since the late 5th century, serving as a transitional figure between the fading Merovingian prestige and the ascendant power of the Carolingian mayors of the palace. His reign is primarily significant not for his own actions, but as the constitutional pivot point for the transfer of royal authority from the traditional Merovingian "do-nothing kings" to the de facto rulers, the Carolingian family, initiating a new era of Frankish and European history.

His ascension to the throne in 743, after a seven-year interregnum following Theuderic IV's death, was orchestrated by Pepin the Short and Carloman, the powerful Carolingian Mayors of the Palace, who sought to legitimize their own authority by installing a Merovingian figurehead. Childeric exercised no real political or military power; true governance rested with the Carolingian brothers. His eight-year reign concluded abruptly in 751 when Pepin the Short, having secured papal approval from Pope Zachary, formally deposed Childeric, tonsured him—a symbolic act of disempowerment and monastic tonsure—and confined him to the monastery of Saint-Bertin.

The deposition of Childeric III fundamentally transformed the political landscape of Francia, ending the Merovingian royal line and formally ushering in the Carolingian dynasty with Pepin the Short's coronation. This event established a new precedent for papal involvement in the legitimization of kingship, solidifying the nascent alliance between the papacy and the Franks that would profoundly shape the future of Western Europe. The shift from a dynastic claim based on ancient lineage to one sanctioned by religious authority laid the groundwork for the Carolingian Renaissance and the eventual Holy Roman Empire.
